questions: Does the drooping of your eyelids become worse after reading or sustained upward gaze?
Does the drooping improve after rest or sleep?
Do you experience double vision?
Do you have difficulty swallowing, speaking, chewing, or breathing?
Do you have weakness in your arms or legs that worsens with activity?
Have your pupils remained the same size during these episodes?
Do your eyelids close involuntarily in repeated spasms?
Do bright lights, wind, stress, or prolonged visual attention trigger or worsen these episodes?
Do you have an uncomfortable urge or sensation in or around the eyes that is relieved by blinking or closing them?
Are you able to keep your eyes open when someone gently holds your eyelids open?
Did these eyelid movements begin after an eye injury, eye surgery, medication, or exposure to drugs that block dopamine?
Are you able to open your eyes normally when asked to do so repeatedly?
Do your eyes open normally during spontaneous activities such as walking, eating, or being startled?
Do you have difficulty initiating other voluntary movements, such as starting to walk or making a saccade to a target?
Have you had any slowness, stiffness, tremor, imbalance, or falls?
Have you had similar episodes of involuntary closure or inability to open the mouth or other muscles?
Are the rapid horizontal eye movements present continuously when you are relaxed and not trying to produce them?
Can you voluntarily start or stop the rapid horizontal eye movements?
Do the eye movements disappear when you are distracted or when you fixate on a target?
Did these symptoms begin after a recent viral illness, fever, or gastrointestinal infection?
Have you had weight loss, night sweats, persistent fever, or any known cancer?
Have you had new headache, confusion, impaired coordination, numbness, or limb weakness?
Do you have sudden, involuntary jerks of your arms, legs, trunk, or face?
Have you had new unsteadiness when walking or difficulty coordinating your limbs?
Have you developed irritability, sleep disturbance, confusion, or other behavioral changes since the illness?
Did the rapid eye movements begin during or within six weeks after the infection?
Have you had episodes of loss of awareness or seizures?
orders: Bedside examination documenting eyelid position, pupil size and reactivity in bright and dim light, and ocular motility.
Bedside apraclonidine 0.5% eye-drop test with reassessment of pupil sizes and eyelid ptosis after 45 minutes.
Ice-pack test applied to each closed upper eyelid for 2 minutes, followed by measurement of the palpebral fissures and assessment for ptosis.
Sustained upgaze test for 2 minutes with repeated assessment of eyelid position and ocular motility.
Repetitive nerve stimulation of the facial and accessory nerves at low frequency.
Comprehensive movement-disorders examination, including assessment for bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor, postural instability, gait, eyelid-opening apraxia, blepharospasm, and levator inhibition.
Examination of vertical and horizontal saccades and smooth pursuit, specifically documenting slowed or restricted vertical saccades and impaired downgaze.
Brain MRI with attention to the midbrain, basal ganglia, and frontal-subcortical regions.
Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal-fluid cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, IgG index, bacterial culture, and CSF PCR for HSV, VZV, enterovirus, and other relevant neurotropic viruses.
Serum and CSF autoimmune/paraneoplastic antibody panels, including anti-Ri, anti-Hu, anti-Ma2, anti-NMDA-receptor, anti-GAD65, anti-DPPX, and anti-GQ1b antibodies.
Serum infectious testing guided by the preceding illness, including HIV, syphilis, Lyme disease, EBV, CMV, and VZV serology/PCR.
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and, if the patient is a child, abdominal/pelvic ultrasound or MRI to screen for occult neuroblastoma or other malignancy.
served: CSF oligoclonal bands and IgG index
